'''''Love Triangle: The Life-Changing Magic of Trigonometry''''' is a 2024 [[non-fiction]] book by [[Matt Parker]]. It examines how applications of [[trigonometry]] have been foundational throughout history, including in contemporary times.

The book was published by [[Riverhead Books]].

== Synopsis ==
In ''Love Triangle'', Matt Parker encourages readers to appreciate the [[geometry]] of [[triangle]]s because it is the foundation of our modern world.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Love Triangle |url=https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/672455/love-triangle-by-matt-parker/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241209005809/https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/672455/love-triangle-by-matt-parker/ |archive-date=2024-12-09 |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=Penguin Randomhouse |language=en-US}}</ref> It offers "practical applications of triangles"<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Roberts |first=Siobhan |date=2024-08-23 |title='Love Triangle' Review: The Magic of Trigonometry |url=https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/books/love-triangle-review-the-magic-of-trigonometry-b634d2dc |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240824021536/https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/books/love-triangle-review-the-magic-of-trigonometry-b634d2dc |archive-date=2024-08-24 |access-date=2024-12-08 |website=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref> in an interesting and humorous narration.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clegg |first=Brian |date=2024-07-10 |title=Love Triangle - Matt Parker **** |url=https://popsciencebooks.blogspot.com/2024/07/love-triangle-matt-parker.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241209005311/https://popsciencebooks.blogspot.com/2024/07/love-triangle-matt-parker.html |archive-date=2024-12-09 |access-date=2024-12-08 |website=Popular Science}}</ref>

The book is divided into ten chapters, titled:

# Going the Distance
# A New Angle
# Laws and Orders
# Meshing About
# Well Fit
# Where Do Shapes Come From?
# Getting Triggy with It
# Where on Earth?
# But Is It Art?
# Making Waves
[[File:Sine Function (One Period).svg|alt=One period of the sine function from 0 to 2pi.|thumb|'''Sine Function (One Period)''']]
An interesting feature of the book is the page numbering system. The introduction begins on page 0.0000000, which is followed by page 0.017452.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Parker |first=Matt |title=Love triangle: how trigonometry shapes the world |date=2024-08-20 |publisher=Riverhead Books |isbn=978-0-593-41812-3 |edition= |location=New York |language=English}}</ref> The decimal numbering continues increasing until 1.0000000 and then decreases to -1.0000000 before increasing back to 0.0000000. The page numbers represent the values of the [[sinusoidal function|sine function]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Calver |first=Tom |date=2024-06-22 |title=Love Triangle by Matt Parker review — why trigonometry rules the world |url=https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/article/love-triangle-matt-parker-review-mprdsbqxx |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=www.thetimes.com |language=en}}</ref> Parker initially wanted to make the book exactly 360 pages long (equal to the number of [[Degree (angle)|degrees]] in a circle); however, the publisher would not agree to that.<ref name=":3">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5q9l9V6N57I |title=Love Triangle and Other Maths (with Matt Parker) |date=2024-08-19 |last=Breaking Math |access-date=2024-12-11 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

==Background==
Matt Parker's initial impetus for writing a book about trigonometry came from his perception that it is "the most advanced math that most people were forced to learn at some point and so it's become this kind of mascot for math is hard and pointless and awful."<ref name=":3" />  He initially proposed a book for the general public about trigonometry approximately ten years prior to the publication of ''Love Triangle''. At that time, his publisher [[Penguin Random House]] were not convinced of the merits of Parker's idea.<ref name=":3" />

When many years later, such a book still had not been published by anyone, Parker was unsure if that market gap needed to be filled or that "it was a terrible idea and that's why no one had done it."<ref name=":3" /> When he began writing ''Love Triangle'', he had a general outline in mind, but worried that he would not have enough chapters or sufficient material for some of the chapters. His concern was unfounded, however, and he ended up having to cut out sections because his research had uncovered "so many amazing stories about geometry and trigonometry."<ref name=":3" />

==Reception==
''Love Triangle'' debuted on [[The New York Times Best Seller list|The New York Times Best Sellers list]] in the category of [[Hardcover]] [[Non-fiction|Nonfiction]] at #14 in the week of September 8, 2024.

Reviewers agree that ''Love Triangle'' is filled with humor. [[Kirkus Reviews]] praises Matt Parker as having "a gift for making somewhat tedious topics not only comprehensible and absorbing, but also great fun."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Love Triangle |url=https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/matt-parker/love-triangle-2/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241215231526/https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/matt-parker/love-triangle-2/ |archive-date=2024-12-15 |access-date=2024-12-15 |website=Kirkus Reviews}}</ref> Terry Freedman found the book to be "full of ‘[[dad joke]]s’ on steroids."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Freedman |first=Terry |date=2024-10-07 |title=Review: Love Triangle: The Life-changing Magic of Trigonometry |url=https://www.ictineducation.org/home-page/review-love-triangle-the-life-changing-magic-of-trigonometry |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241217180857/https://www.ictineducation.org/home-page/review-love-triangle-the-life-changing-magic-of-trigonometry |archive-date=2024-12-17 |access-date=2024-12-17 |website=ICT & Computing in Education |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Opinions on the amount of background [[Mathematics|mathematical]] knowledge the reader needs to enjoy the book are mixed. In a UK review, [[The Times]] acknowledges that "this book is not for everyone" but promises that "those who persevere will end up smarter than they were when they started it."<ref name=":4" /> Siobhan Roberts from the [[The Wall Street Journal|Wall Street Journal]] suggests that "a teacher could easily triangulate numerous fascinating and fun lesson plans from" the book.<ref name=":1" />

== Author biography ==
[[File:Matt Parker at Nine lessons and Carols for Godless People.jpg|alt=Author Matt Parker performing|thumb|'''Matt Parker at Nine Lessons and Carols for Godless People''']]
Matt Parker describes himself as a "stand-up mathematician", combining his career as a [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up comedian]] and his background as a mathematics teacher.<ref name=":1" /> He is from [[Australia]], but now lives and performs in the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Parker |first=Matt |author-link=Matt Parker |title=Things to make and do in the fourth dimension: a mathematician's journey through narcissistic numbers, optimal dating algorithms, at least two kinds of infinity, and more |date=2015 |publisher=Farrar, Straus and Giroux |isbn=978-0-374-53563-6 |location=New York}}</ref> He has authored math articles for ''[[The Guardian]],'' hosted ''[[Outrageous Acts of Science]]'' on the [[Science Channel]], and appeared on several [[BBC]] shows. His [[YouTube]] channel ''Stand-Up Maths'' has over one million views.<ref name=":0" /> He is also the author of ''Things to Make and Do in the Fourth Dimension'' (2014)<ref name=":2" /> and ''Humble Pi: When Math Goes Wrong in the Real World'' (2019).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Parker |first=Matt |title=Humble pi: when math goes wrong in the real world |date=2020 |publisher=Riverhead Books |isbn=978-0-593-08470-0 |location=New York}}</ref>
